question: When a consequential decision is coming up, how much is the reasoning spoken BEFORE the action rather than only as a verdict after it?
pole_low: Acts silently, then gives a one-line verdict on the result
pole_high: Narrates the full plan out loud before touching the controls, so the audience can follow — and dispute — the choice
why: This is the Teacher-vs-Reactor split: plan-first narration makes a run legible and coachable, verdict-only makes it a surprise show. For Coach Player it decides whether a kid can learn strategy from watching, or only be entertained.
evidence_needed: Code the 60 seconds around 10 consequential decisions per creator (boss entry, build choice, route choice): seconds of pre-action reasoning vs post-action comment, in transcripts aligned to gameplay.

question: How deep does the spoken reasoning go — just the chosen move, or the alternatives that were rejected and why?
pole_low: Names only the move being made
pole_high: Walks through branching options, trade-offs, and what would change the decision
why: Deep branching talk creates a character who feels intelligent and teaches decision-making; shallow talk keeps pace but leaves the audience guessing at competence. It also drives session length and rewatch value.
evidence_needed: Sample decision points in roguelike/strategy runs; count distinct alternatives mentioned per decision across Northernlion, CohhCarnage and SplatterCatGaming segments.

question: After a sudden in-game event (jump scare, near-miss, lucky drop), how long is the beat before the first verbal reaction?
pole_low: Instant reaction, overlapping the event itself
pole_high: A held pause — a breath or silence — before any word
why: Reaction latency is a signature: instant reads as high-energy and reactive, a held beat reads as deadpan or genuinely stunned, and it shapes how big the moment feels. Getting it wrong makes an avatar feel either frantic or laggy.
evidence_needed: Measure milliseconds/seconds from event onset in video to first reaction word in timestamped transcripts, for matched event types (deaths, scares, rare drops) across creators.

question: What share of play time is filled with speech versus left to game sound and silence?
pole_low: Sparse — long stretches of pure gameplay, speech reserved for events
pole_high: Near-continuous talk; silence is treated as dead air to be filled
why: Density is the most immediately felt character trait: it sets intimacy, fatigue, and whether a coach's interruption can even get a word in. It also interacts with every other dial.
evidence_needed: Words-per-minute and speech-coverage percentage over full unedited runs or long stream VOD segments, split by combat, travel, and menu time.

question: Is silence ever used DELIBERATELY — before a hard attempt, a scary corridor, a final blow — as a dramatic tool?
pole_low: Never deliberate; any silence is just a gap between thoughts
pole_high: Regularly drops commentary on purpose to build tension before peak moments
why: Deliberate silence is what separates a commentator from a narrator: it signals 'this matters' louder than volume can. An avatar that never shuts up cannot make a moment feel important.
evidence_needed: Find pre-boss / pre-attempt windows and compare speech density there against the same creator's baseline density in the same video.

question: Does the creator's speech pace and energy track the game's tempo, or stay at one personal tempo regardless?
pole_low: One constant personal tempo in menus, travel, and combat alike
pole_high: Speech pace, sentence length, and energy rise and fall with game tempo
why: Tempo-matching makes play feel inhabited and responsive; a constant tempo makes the creator feel like a podcast playing over a game. For an auto-player, tempo-matching is evidence the Personality is actually reading game state.
evidence_needed: Compare words-per-minute and sentence length across coded segments of the same run labelled calm / build-up / crisis; measure the size of the swing per creator.

question: How much commentary is about what is ABOUT to happen — the next threat, goal, or plan — versus only the present moment?
pole_low: Almost entirely present-tense reaction to what is on screen now
pole_high: Constantly previewing: next rooms, upcoming costs, what a find will be used for
why: Lookahead is the audible shape of strategy. High lookahead makes a viewer feel led by someone with a map; low lookahead makes every event a shared surprise. Coach mode needs lookahead or the coach has nothing to steer.
evidence_needed: Classify transcript sentences in sample segments as past / present / future oriented and compare future-share across creators and game genres.

question: When a system or mechanic appears, how much is it explained for a first-time viewer versus left unexplained for insiders?
pole_low: Assumes expertise; mechanics are used, never unpacked
pole_high: Explains systems in plain words as they arise, without stopping play
why: This shades the character between insider companion and guide — and for clever middle-schoolers, explaining the real mechanism IS the appeal. It also decides how portable a creator is across new games.
evidence_needed: Track first encounters with new mechanics in first-look videos (SplatterCatGaming, Wanderbots premieres): was the mechanic explained within a minute of appearing, and in how much depth?

question: At a genuine peak moment — a clutch save, a huge scare, a jackpot — how large is the vocal and physical escalation?
pole_low: Stays almost level; understatement carries the moment
pole_high: Full escalation: volume, speed, laughter or shouting, total commitment
why: Amplitude at peaks is the most cloned trait and the most misjudged: reserved creators make one raised voice feel enormous, high-amplitude creators must keep topping themselves. It sets the avatar's emotional ceiling.
evidence_needed: For matched peak events (deaths, wins, scares), rate volume/pitch/tempo change against that creator's own baseline in the preceding minute — relative, not absolute, escalation.

question: How big does an event have to be before the creator escalates AT ALL?
pole_low: Escalates at small events — minor loot, small mistakes, tiny scares
pole_high: Escalation is rationed; only genuinely big events get a reaction
why: Threshold is what makes escalation mean something: a low threshold is exciting minute-to-minute but inflates away all contrast, a high threshold makes quiet stretches calmer and peaks explosive. The pair (009 threshold, 010 amplitude) defines the whole emotional economy.
evidence_needed: Count escalated reactions per hour divided by total notable events per hour in sample runs; a creator who reacts to 9 of 10 events shades opposite one who reacts to 2 of 10.

question: In horror or high-dread play, how much fear is shown and voiced versus played cool?
pole_low: Downplays fear; jokes or analysis keep distance from it
pole_high: Leans into fear openly — voicing dread, hesitating, reacting bodily
why: Displayed fear is the audience's permission to feel it: high display makes horror communal and funny, low display makes it a mastery watch. It also decides whether an avatar can carry a horror game at all.
evidence_needed: In horror segments (Markiplier, jacksepticeye), count fear-voicing statements, hesitation pauses, and avoidance behaviours per scare versus joke/analysis deflections.

question: When something goes right, how extended is the celebration before play moves on?
pole_low: A brief nod — one line, straight back to work
pole_high: An extended celebration: the moment is replayed in words, savoured, shared with the audience
why: Celebration length teaches the audience what to value. Long celebrations build warmth and ritual; short ones build momentum and respect the viewer's time. It is also a pacing cost an avatar must budget.
evidence_needed: Time from a win event (boss down, rare drop, clutch) to resumption of goal-directed play/speech, averaged over at least 8 wins per creator.

question: When the game is unfair, buggy, or brutally hard, how visibly is frustration vented?
pole_low: Frustration is cooled instantly — reframed as information or a joke
pole_high: Frustration is vented openly and at length before recovery
why: Visible frustration is authenticity for some audiences and poison for others; it also sets how 'safe' the character feels for a young audience. The vent-then-recover arc is itself a character signature.
evidence_needed: Code the 90 seconds after cheap deaths / bugs / lost runs: negative-affect statements, game-directed blame, and time until neutral or positive framing returns.

question: After a failure, where is the cause placed — on the self, or on the game, luck, and circumstances?
pole_low: On the game: luck, design, controls, an unfair moment
pole_high: On the self: the mistake is named plainly as their own
why: Attribution is moral character in miniature. Self-attribution builds trust, growth, and the 'learning to nudge' lesson Coach Player teaches; game-attribution builds comedy and righteous energy but can curdle into excuse-making.
evidence_needed: Classify the first causal statement after each death/failure in sample segments as self / game / luck / mixed, per creator, over at least 15 failures each.

question: How fast and how completely does a failure turn into a next attempt with a plan?
pole_low: The failure is dwelt on — mood drops, the run's energy takes minutes to return
pole_high: Near-instant conversion: one line about the miss, a joke, and a stated recovery plan
why: Recovery speed is resilience made audible, and the single most copyable pro move: audiences stay for the bounce-back, not the perfection. For the avatar it decides whether failure is content or a stall.
evidence_needed: For each failure in sample segments, time until (a) first neutral/positive statement and (b) first forward plan statement; note whether a plan is stated at all.

question: After a meaningful failure, how much forensic debrief happens — what exactly went wrong and what changes next time?
pole_low: No debrief; the next attempt starts clean and unexamined
pole_high: A real breakdown: the causal chain is reconstructed and a specific adjustment is announced
why: Debrief depth shades expert-teacher against pure entertainer, and it is how a character visibly LEARNS — the exact loop the kid coach is supposed to run on the avatar after a session.
evidence_needed: In roguelike/permadeath runs, score debriefs after run-ending deaths: number of causal factors named and whether a concrete next-run adjustment follows.

question: When a safe line and a risky line are both available, which does the creator visibly prefer when nothing forces the choice?
pole_low: The safe, optimal, resource-preserving line
pole_high: The risky line — because it is faster, funnier, or a better story
why: Risk appetite is gameplay character, not just talk: it changes what actually happens on screen. A coach needs this as a true dial because 'be bold' is the most natural kid order there is.
evidence_needed: Find forced-choice moments (low-health pushes, greed rooms, optional hard fights) in sample runs and tally safe vs risky selections, plus whether the risk was announced beforehand.

question: How often does the creator deliberately play the system WRONG — absurd builds, impossible constraints, breaking the intended loop — for the show?
pole_low: Plays the game as designed, mastering its intended systems
pole_high: Regularly misplays on purpose: wrong-way builds, deliberate breakage, scale for its own sake
why: Sabotage is the Let's Game It Out engine: it turns competence into comedy and failure into the product. Too little and a character is earnest; too much and no run ever means anything.
evidence_needed: Per video/hour in sandbox and sim catalogues, classify segments as intended-play vs deliberate misuse; check whether misuse is the video's stated premise or an occasional spice.

question: After repeated failure at the same obstacle, how long does the creator keep attempting before skipping, changing approach, or ending?
pole_low: Bails early — the third failure is the cue to move on
pole_high: Grinds the same obstacle far past the sensible point, and the grind becomes the content
why: Persistence shades stubborn-underdog against efficient-professional, and the grind is where commentary is hardest: nothing new is happening, so character alone carries it.
evidence_needed: Track attempt counts and elapsed time on repeated-failure obstacles (bosses, challenge levels) before strategy change or abandonment, across creators.

question: How is the creator's own skill presented — downplayed as an ordinary player, or displayed as mastery to be admired?
pole_low: Downplayed: played as a fellow amateur, wins are luck, losses are expected
pole_high: Displayed: expertise is named, techniques are demonstrated, mastery is part of the offer
why: Stance decides the audience's relationship: peer or pupil. Downplayed mastery invites participation ('I could do that — and coach that'); displayed mastery invites trust and study. Coach Player wants a character a kid feels able to direct.
evidence_needed: Code self-references to skill in sample segments (luck attributions, technique call-outs, teaching moments) and correlate with how often genuinely expert play is verbally unmarked.

question: During travel, loading, grinding, and other low-event stretches, what fills the time?
pole_low: The downtime is left quiet — travel sounds, occasional remarks
pole_high: Downtime is actively converted: mini-goals, questions, stories, challenges, observations
why: Downtime handling is half the job in real runs and where weak commentators are exposed, because the game stops providing material. What a creator manufactures in a lull IS their character, unassisted.
evidence_needed: Isolate low-event segments of at least 45 seconds in full runs; classify each as silent / game-observation / invented-content, and measure invented-content share per creator.

question: When a tangent starts — a story, a riff, a pop-culture detour — how far from the game does it travel and how long before it returns?
pole_low: Tangents are rare and short; talk stays tethered to the screen
pole_high: Long, fully committed tangents that become the real content of the stretch
why: Tangent depth is Northernlion-style companionship: the game becomes a hearth the conversation sits around. It builds parasocial warmth but risks the play becoming wallpaper.
evidence_needed: Count tangents per hour and their mean duration in long-form runs; note the trigger (lull vs event) and whether the tangent resolves back to a game observation.

question: How are repetitive, mechanically identical stretches — farming, backtracking, resource runs — narrated?
pole_low: Compressed in spirit: talked over minimally, treated as dead time to get through
pole_high: Narrated as process: the rhythm, small variations, and accumulating stakes get named
why: Grind narration decides whether long games are watchable in full or only in highlights. Treating repetition as material creates a meditative, trustworthy character; treating it as dead time creates a highlights-only one.
evidence_needed: In farming/backtracking segments, measure speech density and whether small variations or running totals are verbalised, versus baseline segments from the same run.

question: How directly and how often is the audience addressed — spoken to, asked, thanked, teased — versus talked past as observers?
pole_low: Rarely addressed; the audience overhears a person playing
pole_high: Constantly addressed; viewers are named participants in the session
why: Direct address converts watching into company. Its frequency is one of the strongest levers on whether a solo auto-player feels alone or accompanied — critical when the 'audience' is one kid coach.
evidence_needed: Count second-person addresses and direct questions per 10 minutes across video types (premieres, series episodes, stream VODs) per creator.

question: How much real influence does the audience get over what happens — choices, builds, names, challenges, votes?
pole_low: None; the audience's role is purely to watch a decided performance
pole_high: Real, recurring influence: audience input visibly changes decisions and outcomes
why: This is the DougDoug axis and the seed of Coach Player itself: moving the viewer from spectator toward coach. Where winners cluster tells us how much agency audiences actually reward versus merely praise.
evidence_needed: Catalogue formats per channel: fraction of videos/streams where audience input changed a decision, and whether the change was cosmetic (names) or strategic (builds, routes, rules).

question: How explicitly is a session's premise stated up front — the goal, the gimmick, the experiment — before play begins?
pole_low: No stated premise; play starts and the point emerges, if it does
pole_high: A crisp premise in the first minute: what will be attempted, what would count as success or glorious failure
why: Premise framing is premise awareness as a skill: it gives a run a shape the audience can root for and a failure can be measured against. DougDoug-grade framing turns ordinary play into an experiment with stakes.
evidence_needed: Score the first 60 seconds of sample videos: is a goal/challenge stated, is a success condition implied, and is the premise re-invoked later in the video?

question: Beyond the game's own rules, how much does the creator invent constraints — challenge rules, handicaps, win conditions — to manufacture the show?
pole_low: Plays purely by the game's built-in goals and rules
pole_high: Constantly layers invented rules on top; the invented game inside the game is the show
why: Invented rules are where a pilot stops being a player and becomes a designer. For Coach Player this maps directly onto coach orders: the best creators prove audiences love watching a character operate under a declared, arbitrary constraint.
evidence_needed: Count videos per channel whose stated premise is a self-imposed rule versus the game's default objective; note whether rules are enforced when they start costing the run.

question: When an experiment or plan derails into chaos, does the creator reset and restore order, or commit and ride the derailment?
pole_low: Restores order fast: resets, reloads, re-imposes the plan
pole_high: Commits to the derailment; the wreckage becomes the episode
why: Chaos commitment separates producers from improvisers. Riding a derailment signals trust in one's own commentary to save anything; resetting signals respect for the audience's time and the run's integrity.
evidence_needed: Find derailment moments (experiment failures, run-ending accidents kept in the video): was footage continued to a conclusion or cut/reset, and how was the choice narrated?

question: Where does the humour most often land — on the creator themself, or on the game and its characters?
pole_low: On the self: own mistakes, own fear, own dignity are the material
pole_high: On the game/world: its characters, systems, and absurdities are the material
why: Humour target is likability engineering: self-directed humour makes a character safe to root for and safe for young audiences; world-directed humour is sharper and funnier per line but can shade into cruelty — a rail Coach Player must set deliberately.
evidence_needed: Classify jokes/laugh beats in sample segments by target (self / game system / game character / audience / outside world) and report the self-vs-world ratio per creator.

question: How frequently are jokes or comic framings attempted, independent of whether a funny event occurred?
pole_low: Sparingly — comedy appears only when an event genuinely offers it
pole_high: At a high attempt rate; almost every beat is tested for a comic angle
why: Attempt rate distinguishes a witty player from a comedy act wearing a game. High density guarantees laughs per minute but competes with tension, teaching, and sincerity; low density lets rare jokes land like events.
evidence_needed: Count identifiable joke attempts (setups, comic framings, absurd comparisons) per 10 minutes in matched segment types, not just successful laughs.

question: What is the default vocal register — flat, deadpan understatement, or animated, expressive performance?
pole_low: Deadpan: emotion is minimised in delivery even when events are extreme
pole_high: Animated: delivery is expressive, voiced, and physically performed
why: Register is the fastest identity signal a new viewer gets, and the hardest to fake consistently across a whole run. Deadpan makes chaos funnier by contrast; animation makes emotion contagious.
evidence_needed: Rate delivery on matched event severities across creators using transcript pace/punctuation plus audio energy in clips; check whether register holds under failure as well as success.

question: In a brand-new game, how quickly is a spoken judgement formed — what it is, whether it works, whether it is worth continuing?
pole_low: Judgement is suspended; a long, curious exploration comes before any verdict
pole_high: A verdict forms aloud within the first minutes and is revised in public as play continues
why: SplatterCat-style fast verdicts make a character a trusted filter; suspended judgement makes them a fellow explorer. The shading decides whether the avatar's first minutes in a new game feel like a review or a discovery.
evidence_needed: In premiere/first-look videos, timestamp the first evaluative claim about the game and the first revision of it; compare across curator-style and explorer-style channels.

question: How much does commentary lean on accumulated history — past episodes, old failures, running knowledge of a game or character?
pole_low: Each session stands alone; history is rarely invoked
pole_high: Dense callbacks: past events are treated as shared memory the audience is expected to hold
why: Series memory is retention machinery: it rewards loyalty and makes a character feel continuous — the same property the avatar's memory.md must produce honestly, only citing what actually happened.
evidence_needed: Count callbacks to events outside the current video per hour in series content, and classify as decorative reference vs decision-relevant memory ('last time this killed us, so…').

question: How often does the creator ask genuine questions out loud — to the game, the audience, or themself — and leave space for the answer?
pole_low: Almost never; statements and verdicts dominate
pole_high: Frequently wonders aloud, poses real questions, and lets them hang
why: Question-asking models curiosity for a young audience and is the literal interface of coaching: a character who asks good questions teaches the coach which questions matter. It also creates natural slots for a coach's answer to enter.
evidence_needed: Count interrogative sentences per 10 minutes in transcripts, classified as rhetorical vs genuine (pause follows, audience could answer, creator answers later).

question: When the creator does not know a mechanic, a name, or the right move, how openly is not-knowing admitted and worked through?
pole_low: Not-knowing is covered: bluffed past, edited out, or performed as confidence
pole_high: Not-knowing is narrated openly and investigated live — guessing, testing, and correcting in public
why: This shades scholar against showman, and it is a guardrail-grade trait for an agent aimed at clever kids: an avatar that performs its real uncertainty teaches how to think; one that bluffs teaches bluffing.
evidence_needed: Find first-encounter mechanics and mistakes in unedited runs: is ignorance stated, how is it resolved (test, look-up, audience), and are earlier wrong guesses corrected on record?

question: How explicitly are stakes kept in view — what can be lost, what a resource is worth, how close failure is?
pole_low: Stakes stay implicit; the audience infers danger from events
pole_high: Stakes are narrated continuously: costs, reserves, and consequences are kept verbally on the table
why: Stakes narration is suspense maintenance between events. High narrators make quiet inventory management tense; low narrators rely on the game itself to signal danger. For an auto-player whose coach plans at strategy level, stakes talk IS the strategy feed.
evidence_needed: In survival/roguelike segments, count explicit stake statements (resource levels, loss consequences, distance-to-failure) per 10 minutes and compare with event frequency in the same stretch.

question: How deliberately is a single session shaped into an arc — a beginning goal, a middle complication, an end state — versus played as open-ended time?
pole_low: Open-ended: the session starts and stops with the clock or fatigue
pole_high: Shaped: a goal opens it, progress is tracked aloud, and the ending is framed as a conclusion
why: Arc-shaping is what makes a session rewatchable and a character feel like a protagonist rather than a feed. It is also a pure Personality-layer skill: the Pilot plays the same either way.
evidence_needed: Score sample sessions for stated opening goal, mid-session progress check-ins, and framed endings; compare edited series episodes against raw stream VODs of the same creator.

question: Independent of events, what is the emotional temperature of the default, ordinary minute of play?
pole_low: Cool and dry: ordinary minutes are wry, detached, low-affection
pole_high: Warm and companionable: ordinary minutes feel like playing alongside a friend
why: Baseline warmth — Wanderbots/Cohh territory — is what long sessions are actually made of, since peaks are rare. It decides whether a kid wants this character around for an hour, which is the real retention question.
evidence_needed: Sample ordinary mid-run minutes (no event within 30 seconds) across creators and rate affiliative language: inclusive pronouns, encouragement, gentle humour, expressed enjoyment.

question: Across a channel's life, is the pull toward sampling ever-new games and systems, or returning to deepen mastery of a few?
pole_low: Depth: a few games played for years, mastery and history compounding
pole_high: Novelty: constant first-looks, new systems, breadth over depth
why: This shades explorer against master at the career level, and it drives everything downstream — how much series memory exists, how transferable the teaching is, and what an avatar's own game library should look like.
evidence_needed: From channel catalogues, measure the share of videos in the channel's top 3 games versus the tail; cross-check with premiere-video frequency per month.

question: In audience/AI/coach-controlled formats, how is the handover of control itself handled — as invisible machinery, or as a performed, negotiated part of the show?
pole_low: Invisible: control changes happen backstage; the show pretends seamless authorship
pole_high: Performed: orders, misunderstandings, and negotiations over control are the content, shown and joked about
why: DougDoug proves the negotiation IS entertainment: watching a character receive, misread, and creatively obey an order is funnier than flawless execution. For Coach Player this says the coach-avatar channel should be visible, legible, and played with — not hidden.
evidence_needed: In chat/AI-controlled DougDoug formats and collabs, measure how much runtime is spent explicitly on issuing, clarifying, and reacting to control versus silent execution of it.
